synopsis: The challenge is that one machine may work across 100 or more job sites and applications; chapters repeatedly frame this as a requirement for braking coverage across more than 100 site types, with more than 10 operating scenarios per machine [f16, f283, f5130, f11497]. Combining sites, scenarios, roughly seven weather/light conditions and machine variants exceeds 7,000 validation cells, while finer combinations can reach millions [f5206, f5468, f11331]. Site counts alone are not evidence of coverage: the booklet recommends an auditable taxonomy of sensing- and stopping-relevant attributes, parameterised representative environments anchored to surveyed real sites, and testing of equivalence classes and interactions [f8213, f8214, f3705, f6729]. No single environment-creation method or tool has demonstrated the required breadth in the available time; expert judgment rejects a newcomer’s fully credible all-site, all-weather, all-sensor toolchain by mid-2027, and a four-month simulation window forces low-fidelity sweeps with high fidelity reserved for critical cases [f3699, f8281, f1590, f8871]. Statistical generalisation remains unresolved, with no known exposure distribution for the 100-plus site population; fielded warning-system logs and leave-one-site-type-out validation are proposed ways to improve evidence, not proofs of unrestricted coverage [f2879, f352, f6611, f6995].
